canberra.title: Developer Shane Anderson convicted of criminal contempt over bikie threat to Belconnen project
canberra.snippet: A prominent Canberra developer has been convicted of criminal contempt over a campaign of intimidation against former business partners t...
canberra.content:
Shane Anderson, second from left, at the project sod turning in 2023. Former partners Peter Micolas and Mena Ibrahim stand between MLAs Yvette Berry and Peter Cain. Photo: Zen Photo.

A prominent Canberra developer has been convicted of criminal contempt over a campaign of intimidation against former business partners that included an outlaw motorcycle gang ordering a building site be shut down.

Shane Anderson faced five charges in the NSW Supreme Court brought by fellow developers Peter Micolas and Mena Ibrahim.

Mr Anderson is behind several Canberra property developments and, recently, an AI-generated news site designed to promote his business interests.

The three men were partners in a joint venture to develop The Market Residences in Belconnen, but the latter two had a falling-out with Mr Anderson over his failure to top up his investment and ousted him in 2024.

Mr Anderson took the pair and their associated companies to court, disputing the resolution requiring the cash injection and seeking reinstatement. At stake for Mr Anderson was about $27 million in profit to be reaped from the 10-storey, 326-unit development which is due to be completed in the first quarter of next year.

The case involved a dispute over whether Mr Anderson remained a shareholder and director of Beldev Nominees, whose other shareholder was Mr Ibrahim, after 22 March 2024.

But in May 2025, Mr Micolas and Mr Ibrahim filed a motion accusing Mr Anderson of contempt, including intimidation and attempting to inhibit Mr Ibrahim from defending Mr Anderson’s claim.

The court was told that in December 2024 or January 2025, Mr Anderson had engaged a mediator with strong industry and union ties, known as “Jay”, to help resolve the dispute.

Justice Kate Williams found that Mr Anderson understood this to mean disrupting or threatening to disrupt construction to pressure Mr Ibrahim to abandon his defence and yield to Mr Anderson’s claim to be reinstated as a shareholder and director of Beldev Nominees.

At about 5:30 am on 30 January 2025 at The Markets site, Icon employee Mr A was confronted by five or six men wearing balaclavas and clothing bearing the words “Finks” and “Finks MC”.

One of the men called “Matthew” said: “We’ve been sent here by Shane Anderson. He needs to be reinstated as a partner of this development. You can send this message to the other partners. If Shane is not reinstated, this job will be shut down. We don’t want any trouble, so I trust you’re not going to call the police.”

They left but said they would be back.

The Markets Residences in Belconnen, where bikies tried to shut down the site last year. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The next morning between 20 and 25 men surrounded the site. Mr A observed that they had formed a line, and it reminded him of union-style picketing.

One of the men told Mr A: “This development site is closed until Shane Anderson is reinstated as a shareholder. He has been wronged.”

The man told Mr A “we can do this the easy way or the hard way. You will need to ring Jay and sort it out”.

Mr A called police and when they arrived, the men left, some getting into a Mercedes with Finks plates.

In a phone conversation, Jay repeated to Mr A that Mr Anderson had been wronged and it was affecting his business. “The site will be closed until then.”

A Mr B, an Icon director, had a similar conversation with Jay.

Justice Williams said that in response to Mr B’s expression of concern for the welfare of Icon staff and subcontractors, Jay replied that “there won’t be a problem as long as Shane Anderson is reinstated as a shareholder”, implying that there was a risk to the welfare of any staff and subcontractors who attempted to enter the site if Mr Anderson was not reinstated as a shareholder.

CCTV footage confirmed the early-morning visits, and evidence from a digital forensics and cybersecurity expert corroborated the phone conversations and calls between Jay and Mr Anderson, including a photograph sent of site workers.

Justice Williams rejected submissions that disrupting the site would amount to self-sabotage by Mr Anderson, that Jay had taken it upon himself to try to shut down the site without Mr Anderson’s knowledge, or that it was a matter of miscommunication rather than Mr Anderson’s intention.

“As a matter of practical reality, Jay’s unlawful actions, which Mr Anderson caused, put at risk and threatened to put at continuing risk the progress of the development which was carrying significant liabilities, and thereby put at risk the potential profits that Mr Ibrahim and interests associated with him stood to make from the development,” he said.

“The threat conveyed was plain: reinstate Mr Anderson so that he will share in the profits, or the site will remain closed. That threat had a real and definite tendency to interfere with the course of justice in these proceedings by exerting pressure on Mr Ibrahim to yield to the threat by abandoning the defence of Mr Anderson’s claims and abandoning his reliance on the court to resolve the legal dispute between Mr Anderson and Beldev SA and the active defendants.”

Justice Williams found Mr Anderson guilty of all charges beyond reasonable doubt and set down 9 September for a directions hearing on sentencing.

canberra.title: Snow Concert Hall scores major artistic coup with Dutch piano superstars Lucas and Arthur Jussen
canberra.snippet: In a massive artistic coup for the national capital, the most in-demand piano duo of a generation is landing in Canberra for their first ...
canberra.content:
Dutch pianists Lucas and Arthur Jussen are headed to Canberra following their performance at London’s Royal Albert Hall for BBC Proms. Photo: BBC Proms/ Chris Christodoulou.

In a massive artistic coup for the national capital, the most in-demand piano duo of a generation is landing in Canberra for their first major Australian tour, fresh off performing at London’s Royal Albert Hall for the legendary BBC Proms.

The arrival of Dutch brothers Arthur and Lucas Jussen — widely regarded as the most famous classical musicians to ever emerge from Holland — marks a monumental shift for local audiences, according to Snow Concert Hall Artistic Director Ana de la Vega.

“It’s so exciting to welcome the Jussens to Australia, and the fact that they’re performing in Canberra is especially satisfying,” she says.

“Normally, artists like this travel exclusively to Sydney, Melbourne, or Brisbane. Having them in our backyard, it feels like the vision we had for Snow Concert Hall three years ago has come to life.”

But it’s not only the location that has music lovers buzzing — it’s the almost mythic connection we’re about to witness.

What makes the Jussens one of the world’s most captivating duos isn’t just their extraordinary technique.

“They are celebrated for having an almost telepathic musical bond, the kind that only comes from performing together since childhood,” Ana says.

There’s an inevitability to that connection. Raised by musician parents, both brothers started playing at age five and, from Arthur’s very first keystrokes, always together.

“I would always listen to my parents and Lucas practising together, and from the first moments, I knew I also wanted to play, wanted to follow my big brother,” Arthur says.

“We never really decided, ‘We’re going to become a duo’ … We had the same piano teacher, we lived in the same house, so she said, ‘Why don’t you play together?’

“It felt very natural, and I think the beautiful thing was that we enjoyed very much making music together, to sit side by side behind the piano and create these beautiful sounds.”

Side by side, the brothers grew into a global phenomenon.

“They have cultivated an unbelievable symbiosis that makes them so magnetic and just astounds audiences,” Ana says.

The Jussens performed at BBC Proms under the baton of conductor Kazuki Yamada. Photo: BBC Proms/ Chris Christodoulou.

The Jussens were accompanied by CBSO Chorus, Sydney Philharmonia Choirs and City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra. Photo: BBC Proms/ Chris Christodoulou.

The brothers are celebrated for having an almost "telepathic" musical bond. Photo: Sanja Marusic.

The Jussens have performed internationally since debuting at ages 10 and 13 in Amsterdam’s prestigious Concertgebouw.

While they made a whirlwind trip to Sydney eight years ago, travelling with the Dutch royal family to perform at the Sydney Opera House, this marks their first full Australian tour.

Crucially, while their other Australian dates feature grand orchestras, their Snow Concert Hall performance offers a rare 90-minute intimate recital.

“This is not just any concert. It’s a chance to experience two world-leading pianists perform a magnificent program together in an intimate hall where every nuance can be heard without the cover of an orchestra,” Ana says.

The program pairs the delicacy of Mozart with the dramatic intensity of Schubert, before building to Mendelssohn and a four-hands arrangement of Stravinsky’s Le Sacre du Printemps, performed with a unique twist.

“A four-hand work is most often played on two instruments; here we will have four hands on one instrument,” Ana explains.

“They’ll be playing on a stunning Steinway Model D that the late great Terry Snow and I managed to get for the hall. A piano needs to match its hall, and this one is perfect for Snow Concert Hall. We’ve never had four hands on it, and hearing what comes out of it in the hands of the Jussens will be very exciting.”

The Jussens are known for their seamless versatility. Audiences never know who will take the upper or lower register, or lead on piano one versus piano two.

But even after decades together, Lucas notes audiences can still expect genuine surprises on stage.

“Things happen that weren’t planned, and this might sound a little strange, but sometimes those are the nicest moments,” Lucas says.

“Out of something that initially feels like a mistake, something can happen musically that’s actually very nice. We are not perfect … So every concert is different and spontaneous, and I think it should be that way.”

Ultimately, the hope is audiences will be able to close their eyes and hear what sounds like the skill of two artists rolled into one.

“When we play together, I’m listening to Lucas literally every millisecond, and I try to feel where he wants to go, what he wants to do, how he plays, his tone,” Arthur says.

“There can be no ego when we play together … Sometimes I follow Lucas, sometimes he follows me, and the will to adapt to each other is very important.”

Lucas & Arthur Jussen perform at the Snow Concert Hall on Friday, 28 August, at 7 pm.

canberra.title: ANU gets its heart back as University House reopens to the public
canberra.snippet: Six years and $121 million later, the Australian National University finally has its heart back – just in time for its 80th birthda...
canberra.content:
Master of University House Peter Kanowski (in the Great Hall) says the ANU’s heart is back. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Six years and $121 million later, the Australian National University finally has its heart back – just in time for its 80th birthday.

University House was one of the buildings damaged in the devastating 2020 hailstorm, which saw thousands of cars written off, homes destroyed and about 80 per cent of the ANU campus damaged.

Master of University House, Professor Peter Kanowski, said the building’s age simply meant it couldn’t withstand the original storm, exposing the interior to the elements.

“We’ve got something like 64,000 bespoke roof tiles, and they were more or less 70 years old, and they didn’t stand up to the hailstorms,” he explained.

“All of those tiles got cracked by the hail, so when it rained a few weeks later, the water penetrated the ceiling down through the building, took out the fire system, the building had to be evacuated, and then came COVID.

“And so the building sat empty for two years with only possums living here until the university and its insurers agreed on how we’d repair it.”

It’s taken about 1500 workers to repair the building.

Asbestos, lead and mould damage needed to be remediated before works could even begin. This was followed by the restoration of each roof tile and the replacement of the copper panelling. All the gas pipes were removed, and the building completely electrified and brought up to standard with modern building codes.

Inside, leather and wood panelling needed to be revived and all the damaged furniture painstakingly brought back to life.

Books and artworks weren’t spared, but they’re also back to their original states.

“University House has been the ceremonial heart of the ANU since it was opened in 1954, and for the last six-and-a-half years we haven’t had that heart,” Prof Kanowski said.

“It’s been a hole in the life of the campus, and it’s so wonderful to be back and open again.”

University House includes a Great Hall decorated by the Leonard French mural ‘Regeneration’, multiple recreation and dining rooms (including a famous beer garden), 97 bookable hotel rooms and 60 rooms for postgraduate students.

They feature Fred Ward-designed and built furniture, and the original underfloor heating in the bathrooms.

The building was designed by Professor Brian Lewis and awarded the 1953 Sulman Medal for Architectural Merit.

His son David Lewis (who was seven when the building was originally opened) described University House’s closure as a “deprivation” for both ANU and the community.

“[Having it open again] is obviously great because it adds to the atmosphere … [provides a chance] to meet other people and that’s a real pleasure,” he said.

University House has been painstakingly restored inside and out following the 2020 hailstorm. Photos: Claire Fenwicke.

Design and oversight of the restoration was undertaken by heritage architects Lovell Chen and the building work by Hindmarsh Construction Australia.

Lovell Chen’s Audrey Ong said the building’s simplicity actually made restoration even more challenging.

“Trying to restore the original heritage fabric was a challenge, but there was a lot of research that went into understanding the materiality, understanding the methodology, and trying to faithfully restore and repair that,” she said.

“Some of the original heritage fabric on the building includes … terracotta tiles, parquetry flooring, leather panelling, wood leather panelling, to the walls, acoustic ceiling tiles, so they are very specialised trades.”

The asbestos, lead and mould remediation – along with the extent of the damage – meant many parts of the building essentially had to be stripped back to its shell.

Hindmarsh Construction’s project manager, Alex Morgan, said workers touched every area of the project.

“We needed to take the building apart before we could put it back together and start the restoration,” he said.

“It was very fulfilling to be able to bring it back to where it used to be.”

To prevent similar damage in the future, waterproofing membranes have been installed.

Most of the building’s repairs were covered by insurance, with the rest paid from funds ANU had already set aside for infrastructure.

Prof Kanowski said this opening was another healing moment for the university.

“The ANU community’s getting back a place where they can meet, formally and informally, to relax, interact with people that you don’t see in your day-to-day role, whatever that happens to be, and that’s already started to happen,” he said.

“The bar’s been open for four days and [already] people were moving furniture around down in the bar and just reoccupying the building.

“It’s given the university a special place to welcome the community back that we haven’t had for the last six-and-a-half years.”

University House will be officially reopened on Friday, 14 August, ahead of an ANU campus community day on Saturday, 15 August.

canberra.title: RSPCA ACT’s Pets of the Week: Bindi and Smee
canberra.snippet: Dog of the Week: Bindi Some readers will be thinking, “I thought this dog was adopted already?” Yes, Bindi was on a trial adoption after ...
canberra.content:
7 August 2026

Start the conversation

Bindi’s a real sweetheart. Photo: RSPCA ACT.

Dog of the Week: Bindi

Some readers will be thinking, “I thought this dog was adopted already?” Yes, Bindi was on a trial adoption after spending around one year at our shelter. Unfortunately, she’s back with us.

But as we learn more, we can share more.

First, the things we already knew: She’s a gentle sweetheart who truly loves her people. In fact, she lived very gently with children, and she’s a people pleaser. A calm and lovable dog.

Walking her is a tough proposition, though. She’s very reactive to other dogs and wildlife, so when a stray rabbit zooms past, you’ll need to be aware. That was the biggest thing with her unsuccessful trial. Quite a small thing in the scheme of things, but hopefully it helps us find her a forever home this time around.

We know there’s a dog lover out there just right for this darling girl. Is it you?

Smee isn’t afraid to show her love. Photo: RSPCA ACT.

Cat of the Week: Smee

Lots of cats are currently available for adoption, including kittens. The annual ‘Kitten Season” in the warmer months certainly brings in more kittens to our shelter, but honestly, the steady stream, despite winter, has not stopped.

Little Smee here is a great example of the brilliance of our foster care community. Smee was a stray and, like all strays, was very shy and uncertain when he arrived; very unsure around people.

Smee has grown into a lovely boy. He’s affectionate, and when he’s adjusted to you (give him a moment), he’ll be rubbing against your legs and showing love in no time.

Visit Smee and our other lovely cats at RSPCA ACT; there’s sure to be a cat or kitten just perfect for you.

Pawnotes: Several months ago, 17 pups arrived on our doorstep at the same time. After foster care, medication treatment, vaccinations, desexing and care, almost all have been adopted. Thank you, Canberra!

Animal viewing hours

Monday to Saturday: 10 am to 3 pm

Sundays and public holidays: Closed.

If you’re interested in meeting RSPCA ACT’s incredible animals with a view to adoption, please drop by our shelter today. And get to know all the other awesome animals at RSPCA ACT.

canberra.title: Ainslie home sets new standards for design excellence and efficient living
canberra.snippet: A masterclass in home architecture and passive design, 99 Duffy Street is a four-bedroom, four-bathroom one-of-a-kind property in Ainslie...
canberra.content:
Fronting the street with an inviting blue colour scheme, this home is every bit as unique on the inside. Photos: Home.by Holly.

A masterclass in home architecture and passive design, 99 Duffy Street is a four-bedroom, four-bathroom one-of-a-kind property in Ainslie that sets the standard for smart homes.

It’s clear from the get-go that this property has been designed for impact, fronting the street with European larch shingles, a unique colour scheme and shroud-edge windows. But what’s hidden are the technical and structural inclusions.

“This is a home built to the rigorous standards of a German PassivHaus, designed by Adhami Pender Architecture, which means that it’s energy efficient, comfortable, intelligent and beautiful!” Home.by Holly agent Holly Komorowski says.

Features include double insulation, an 8.8 kW solar array, Zehnder heat recovery system, a thermal banking slab and German-engineered triple-glazed windows, all of which take advantage of a north-facing aspect.

“It’s engineered to perform at the highest energy star rating, which obviously means that running the home is cost-effective, while utilising the most sophisticated control systems,” Holly says.

But the design is about more than efficiency. The architect has created a beautiful place to live, cleverly laid out across two floors, with multiple living spaces and two main suites.

“Once you step in the front door, you’re met by the main living space. It has a warm, farmhouse feel, with plenty of organic materials and the dining/kitchen space is separated from the living space by a prominent stone wall,” Holly says.

This clever method of separation creates an aesthetically pleasing delineation between the dining space, which is more intimate, and the living space, which feels expansive thanks to a clerestory space and high windows.

“This home exemplifies architecture at its finest – the kind that feels so effortless and intuitive that it almost goes unnoticed,” Holly says.

Like the rest of the property, the kitchen beautifully blends a design that pleases the eye with practicality. A large window drenches the space in light, and the long island bench and window nook make for ideal conversation spaces.

“The seamless connection between the kitchen, mudroom and garage was designed to support the rhythm of daily life, whether it’s bringing in groceries, unpacking school bags or heading out the door in the morning,” Holly says.

Private spaces include two separate main suites, each with beautifully finished ensuite bathrooms and walk-in robes, enhancing the potential for multi-generational living or hosting guests.

“The main suite features a striking internal window that overlooks the double-height living room void, allowing natural light to filter deep into the space,” Holly says.

Bedrooms also benefit from vaulted ceilings, creating plenty of space and light.

A private study with fixed joinery, a floating desk and custom lighting provides a perfect place to work from home, set up a home library or do home projects.

A similar level of care has been taken with the outdoor spaces too, which are simply exceptional.

“There’s a cosy alfresco area with a wood fire, an integrated pizza oven and cafe blinds. But that’s not the half of it. There’s also a grassed area, a sitting space and, of course, the heated pool with a spa,” Holly says.

The property also boasts a wine cellar, device-controlled lights, CCTV, windows and irrigation, a double carport and double garage.

And the location takes the cake, being literally a street away from the Mount Ainslie Reserve, with easy access to walking trails and green spaces.

“Ainslie shops are also just a few streets away. You couldn’t ask for a better combination of daily peace and access to amenities,” Holly says.

“This home is on another level. Every space has been designed to impress, every detail feels elevated, and there’s not a single box left unticked. It’s the kind of property that doesn’t just meet expectations – it completely redefines them.”

For more information on 99 Duffy Street in Ainslie, contact Holly Komorowski. And to stay ahead of the market, check out the latest listings on Zango.

australia.title: Dogs to be euthanised after man dies following suspected animal attack at rural Sydney property
australia.snippet: Police say body of 23-year-old found at Eschol Park property with significant injuries, indicating he may have been attacked before death...
australia.content:
A group of dogs has been taken to a shelter to be euthanised after a young man died following a suspected dog attack at a rural Sydney property.

Authorities were alerted to the discovery of the 23-year-old’s body at a rural property in Sydney’s south-west on Wednesday. Police found the body with what they described as significant injuries and established a crime scene.

“Initial inquiries indicate the man may have been attacked by animals prior to his death,” New South Wales police said in a statement.

Campbelltown investigators and council rangers attended an Eschol Park property on Friday morning and seized five dogs, who were taken to the animal shelter to be euthanised, police said.

According to Sydney radio station 2GB, none of the animals were registered or microchipped.

NSW police said a 53-year-old man was also treated at the scene for a minor hand injury.

The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, said the reasons behind the 23-year-old’s presence at the house was unclear.

“We don’t know the circumstances by which the male was on the premises,” he told reporters.

“He certainly doesn’t appear to be a resident of that location.”

Guardian Australia understands the incident occurred at a house on Badgally Road known as Saturn’s Rings or the Universal Power House.

Based on the rings of Saturn, the circular building was designed by Stefan Dzwonnik in the 1970s and intended to serve as a home for him and his family, according to the Campbelltown City Library.

But Saturn’s Rings was never completed, and Dzwonnik died in 2018, according to the library.

The Campbelltown council said it was assisting police.

“Council is supporting police inquiries and will continue to assist as required, in accordance with its legislative responsibilities, including determining the registration and ownership status of the dogs,” a spokesperson said.

Inquiries are ongoing and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

Achol Arok contributed reporting

australia.title: Alan Jones trial: complainant wants to ‘humiliate’ broadcaster by revealing intimate details of alleged assaults, defence tells court
australia.snippet: Barrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent...
australia.content:
Alan Jones’s defence barrister has told a Sydney court one of the broadcaster’s alleged victims invented details of alleged indecent assaults at a Fitzroy Falls farm to “humiliate” and “smear” the former media titan.

Complainant J told the court during evidence-in-chief earlier this week that during one alleged incident in the property’s bedroom, Jones’s penis was not fully erect and “not very big”.

On Friday, J, during cross-examination, denied fabricating his account of alleged indecent assaults at Jones’s farm in the southern highlands more than 20 years ago.

Complainant J, aged in his 40s, is the first alleged victim to give evidence in the trial at Downing Centre local court. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges involving six men.

J this week alleged in court he did not consent to a kiss near the farm’s pigsty, the touching of his penis on a lounge room couch or sexual touching in the guest bedroom.

Under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, complainant J on Friday denied inventing details about Jones’s genitals to humiliate the older man.

Bashir asked: “This account you’ve given of ‘penis wiggling’ is an attempt to humiliate Mr Jones, isn’t it?”

“No,” J replied.

Bashir suggested in court that it was “an attempt to smear him, isn’t it?” J again said: “No.”

J has previously alleged that when visiting the farm as a teenager, he heard a “tap, tap, tap” before Jones came into the bedroom. He told the court that, while they were both wearing robes, Jones wiggled his hips so their penises crossed.

Bashir said: “You cast yourself as ‘impressive’ and Alan as not achieving an erection as part of the humiliation you are trying to describe, didn’t you? So too your comment on Tuesday that ‘it wasn’t very big’.”

“No,” J replied in court on Friday.

Bashir alleged: “You wouldn’t know because you have never seen Mr Jones’s penis.”

Complainant J then said: “Yes, I have.” J said that Jones had remarked that the then teenager’s penis was “impressive”.

He had earlier told the court that Jones’s penis was circumcised and his genitals were hairy. Bashir suggested that he guessed the details because circumcision was likely for an “Anglo-Saxon man of his age – and so too the hair on the genitals”.

J disagreed that he had guessed.

Throughout the cross-examination, Bashir alleged that J was forgetting key details because he had made the whole thing up.

Bashir told the court: “Are you making your evidence up as you go along?”

“No,” complainant J replied.

Bashir challenged J’s memory of his visits to the southern highlands property in the mid-2000s, suggesting in court that he had mixed up occasions, dates and fellow guests.

J agreed that his family was invited to visit the property, and he accompanied them. Bashir said there were inconsistencies in his police statement and his evidence in court regarding how many nights he stayed and which vehicle he drove.

Bashir questioned J in detail about an alleged kiss by Jones while the two men were looking at a pigsty on the farm.

Bashir told the court: “There was no kiss at the pigsty. It was a fabrication.”

J replied: “No, it wasn’t.”

The defence barrister said if J was afraid of being assaulted, as he claimed, he didn’t have to walk into the lounge room wearing a robe after Jones instructed him to shower and come back wearing the robe and nothing else.

She pointed to inconsistencies between his police statement and evidence-in-chief.

Bashir said: “There is nothing in your statement about a robe.” J replied: “I remember he was in a robe.”

Bashir suggested he read about Jones wearing a robe in the media. J denied this but agreed there was no mention of Jones wearing a robe in his statement.

The defence barrister said J’s account of the alleged assaults did not make sense because he was young and fit – and he could have pushed the older Jones away.

Bashir asked if Jones had ever threatened to withdraw his stipend and J said no.

Bashir said: “He never said to you he would pull the money if you didn’t do what he wanted, did he?” J replied: “No.”

J agreed that there were “no repercussions” when he couldn’t make invitations from Jones and that Jones didn’t ask him for favours in return for financial support

Bashir said: “All Mr Jones asked of you was that you dedicate yourself to your career.” J told the court: “That’s not all he asked me.”

Bashir closed her cross-examination with two final questions.

Bashir said: “Alan Jones never kissed you indecently.”

J replied: “Yes, he did”

Bashir said: “Alan Jones never indecently touched you.”

J said: “Yes, he did.”

The trial continues on Tuesday with J returning to the witness stand for a sixth day for a re-examination by the crown. There is a break in evidence on Monday.

australia.title: Census 2026 Australia: when is it, will it be online and why does it matter? Everything you need to know
australia.snippet: One expert says the survey, to be held on the night of 11 August, could be Australia’s most progressive, with new questions on sexuality ...
australia.content:
On 11 August, millions of Australians will simultaneously complete the same 66-question survey.

Held every five years, the census will record important details about each person to help inform the country – including governments – about Australia’s demographics.

But there are changes taking effect this year, including new questions about gender and sexuality, which one expert says will make it “probably the most progressive census Australia has ever seen”.

Here are some things you should know about Australia’s 2026 census.

australia.title: Attorney general warns women and children at risk of ‘harmful conduct’ from smartglasses users – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Federal parliament is returning from winter break next week. Do you have a question you’d like to ask Guardian Au...
australia.content:
Attorney general writes to privacy commissioner about smartglasses concerns

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has written to the privacy commissioner over potential concerns surrounding smartglasses.

Rowland said the products, which are growing in popularity, had significant implications, especially for women and children who could be disproportionately affected by “inappropriate recording, harassment, surveillance or other harmful conduct”.

Rowland said in a statement:

Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear.

Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.

The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age.

  • The Alan Jones trials continued at Downing Centre local court, with complainant J, the first alleged victim, continuing to give evidence.

  • Atlassian’s share price has surged after the Sydney-founded software giant beat investor expectations with stronger-than-predicted financial results.

  • South Australia’s Royal Adelaide Show has cancelled all bird shows and exhibits as H5 bird flu numbers continue to rise. The state has recorded 119 out of 155 cases nationally. In Victoria, a temporary housing order for chicken and egg producers with 50 or more birds has been introduced.

  • The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has written to the privacy commissioner over potential concerns surrounding smartglasses days after Kmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia.

  • Travellers on domestic and international flights at Sydney airport have faced major delays and cancellations after Airservices Australia reported “operational restrictions to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands”.

  • The federal inquiry into racism, hatred and violence directed at Indigenous peoples is continuing in Melbourne, with unions and national education and training organisations giving evidence.

Thanks for joining us, have a lovely weekend!

Penry Buckley

Second NSW Liberal frontbencher expected to give evidence to Icac

The NSW shadow finance minister, Eleni Petinos, will give evidence to Icac, making her the second Liberal frontbencher to appear before the commission’s Operation Rosny following the state’s shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope.

The NSW opposition and Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, has confirmed Petinos, who is on maternity leave, is expected to appear before the commission. In an interview with 2GB, she said:

Well, [Petinos] is a witness, but she’s assisting the inquiry. She’s not a person of interest. I would encourage any of my team or people within the Liberal party or outside of the Liberal party to assist the inquiry to help provide support their evidence. That doesn’t mean they’ve done anything wrong … And you know, if anything comes up that isn’t that, then I’ll consider it at the time.

The second allegation being investigated by the corruption watchdog is that between 2020 and 2023, fugitive property developer Jean Nassif made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Liberal figures in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif, including the removal of the then building commissioner, David Chandler.

On its first day, the inquiry heard an October 2021 phone call featuring Nassif, in which he allegedly claimed he had paid for Chandler’s removal, and that “the fair trading minister is gonna to be one of my girls”.

The inquiry heard that two months after the call, the then Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet appointed Petinos as fair trading minister in a reshuffle. In July 2022, Chandler handed in his resignation following an investigation into his conduct that had been requested by Petinos, which later cleared him of any wrongdoing.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC said evidence would determine if Nassif’s call was “an incidence of wishful thinking that serendipitously came to pass” or the result of work by conservative factional group the Reformers. Perrottet and Petinos have not been named in Icac’s allegations and are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Catie McLeod

Progressive ‘Free Palestine Party’ thwarted in bid to rival right-wing provocateur Avi Yemini’s party using similar name

The would-be progressive “Free Palestine Party” has been knocked back in its attempt to stop right-wing provocateur Avi Yemini from using the name “Free Palestine” to funnel votes to conservatives.

The Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) sent out a press release earlier today, stating it had refused the application by the “Free Palestine Party” to register as a political party.

The VEC said it was required by law to refuse the application because the party’s name resembled that of an unrelated recognised political party, causing likely confusion or mistake.

In this case, “Free Palestine Party” resembled the name of the registered political party “Free Palestine”, the VEC said.

It might seem confusing, but the latter party, “Free Palestine”, is a separate entity, linked to Yemini. It was formally recognised by the VEC on Wednesday.

Yemini, a former Israeli soldier and self-styled investigative journalist who creates content for his YouTube channel, Rebel News Australia, applied to register “Free Palestine” as a political party with the VEC on 2 May.

When he announced his plans for the party in April, Yemini said he would use it to funnel votes to conservative parties and “flow our preferences on to parties that want to free Palestine from Hamas” at the November state election.

In response, a counter-group calling itself the “Free Palestine Party” was set up. Guardian Australia has contacted the group for comment.

According to its website, its creation was “spurred on by Avi Yemini’s plot to create a fake ‘Free Palestine’ party to deceive Victorian electors at the next state election”.

The “Free Palestine Party” applied to register with the VEC on 2 June, a month after Yemini lodged his application to register “Free Palestine”.

You can read more about Yemini’s plans here:

Victoria requires poultry farms to house chickens as bird flu cases rise

Petra Stock

The Victorian government has introduced a temporary housing order for chicken and egg producers with 50 or more birds, in a precautionary step to protect the poultry industry from H5 bird flu.

The measure, which will apply for an initial 14 days, will affect hundreds of businesses in Melbourne and along coastal areas.

The state’s agriculture minister, Michaela Settle, said the proactive approach was introduced to ensure that eggs and chicken remained affordable for consumers.

We’re working proactively to ensure that eggs and poultry are protected, and that Victorians can continue to afford and find them on the shelves.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has assured free range farmers that they would be able to continue to use the free range label.

Victoria has recorded 47 positive cases in wild birds, with new detections at Yambuk, Apollo Bay and Clyde, a south-eastern suburb of Melbourne.

There is currently no detection of H5N1 bird flu in poultry in Victoria or in Australia.

Andrew Messenger

Second-year constable praised as “hero” cop for rescuing toddler from Charleville siege

A second-year constable who rescued a toddler from a siege in Charleville while in “grave danger” has been praised as a hero cop.

The 18-month-old child’s mother died at a house in the regional town, after police arrived to reports of a serious assault on Wednesday evening.

The southern region assistant commissioner, Matthew Vanderbyl, said police were confronted by Michael Waltke, who they believed to be armed, and were in grave danger.

Vanderbyl said the child appeared in a doorway covered in someone else’s blood. She was “scooped up” by a male officer who took her to safety, he said.

“That police officer took that distressed child and did what anybody who has young children or knows young children would do, and just held that child close to his chest, and turned himself away from the scene of danger,” Vanderbyl said.

The officers then “quite rightly” withdrew to a safe distance, Vanderbyl said.

“You have to feel for a child who has potentially seen what I … suspect that she has seen in that scene,” he said.

Expert forensic police are still at the scene, and the investigation continues.

Andrew Leigh backs ACCC inquiry into alleged food mislabelling allegations

The assistant minister for competition, Andrew Leigh, a has welcomed the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission’s (ACCC) confirmation that it will investigate allegations of food mislabelling raised by an ABC Four Corners report.

In statement on Friday, the ACCC said it had “initiated inquiries” into the claims. The ACCC Commissioner, Luke Woodward, said:

It is important that consumers can be confident that any claims made on food labelling, packaging and in advertisements are truthful, accurate and not misleading.

We know that consumers may be guided by non-price factors, including claims about the country of origin or supply chain, when choosing which food products to buy.

At a press conference, Leigh echoed his comments on the inquiry’s importance:

Australians shouldn’t be duped by misleading labels. Australians should be able to walk into a store and know that what it says on the tin is accurate.

VIC Liberal party endorses Roshena Campbell to replace Moira Deeming ahead of election

The Victorian Liberal Party has endorsed Roshena Campbell as its Upper House candidate for the Western Metropolitan Region.

Campbell replaces Moira Deeming, who was removed as a candidate after a state party vote following a legal saga stemming from an assault allegation she made against former leader Matthew Guy.

Campbell, who now serves as Melbourne’s current deputy lord mayor, will appear on the top spot on the Liberals’ upper house ticket this November. She said in a statement:

This State is broken. And I want to be part of the team with the experience and the Plan to fix it.

The West is the heart of multicultural Victoria, and I am passionate about ensuring our multicultural communities are heard and supported.

I’m proud to join Jess Wilson’s new Liberal Team in the West, to finally deliver the West’s fair share.

Penry Buckley

NSW opposition leader will ‘let privileges committee do its work’ after two Liberals referred over Reformers allegations

The NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, has again backed Damien Tudehope after he became one of two Liberals referred to the parliamentary privileges committee following allegations they aided a factional group under investigation by the corruption watchdog.

Yesterday afternoon, the NSW upper house voted to refer Liberal MLCs Damien Tudehope and Chris Rath to the privileges committee, in a motion unopposed by the opposition, after allegations they aided members of conservative factional group the Reformers during a parliamentary inquiry in 2023.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) is investigating whether members of the Reformers allegedly solicited or accepted illegal donations in order to recruit or renew members to the Liberal party, a practice known as “branch stacking”, which is not illegal.

Tudehope, who has stepped aside from his roles as shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house after being called as a witness in Icac’s inquiry, on Tuesday admitted to the watchdog he leaked a confidential draft parliamentary inquiry report on the allegations to a member of the Reformers in 2023.

Last week, the Sydney Morning Herald reported that Rath helped members of the Reformers evade summons during the parliamentary inquiry that preceded Icac’s investigation. He received a caution from the privileges committee at the time, but yesterday marks his second referral over the same issue. Following yesterday’s vote, Rath, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, apologised again for the incident. Tudehope, who has not been named in Icac’s allegations, was absent from the chamber.

Asked if she would take action following Tudehope’s referral at a press conference today, Sloane said:

I’ll wait for the finding of that, and I don’t have that yet. Damien is on the backbench for the duration of the ICAC inquiry, and I’m not going to run parallel inquiries; I’ll let the privileges committee do its work and we’ll see what they say.

Sarah Collard

Continuing from last post …

Frank Gaffer, a First Nations organiser with the Victorian branch of the Australian Education Union, said that before 2026 there was no way for teachers in public schools to report racist incidents.

Prior to this year, if you were to report racism as a staff member of a school, you had to report it under the option of other or psychosocial safety, but there was no actual data collection of racism for educators within public schools.

But current reporting mechanisms can also be unsafe, said Kimberley Reed, also from the Australian Education Union, who told the committee that lodging a complaint or an incident could lead to further harm.

Reporting it can actually lead to further incidences of racism because often Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are the only staff member in their school, so if someone has made a report of racism and it’s addressed with the person, whether they’re named or not, people know exactly where it came from.

Racism inquiry hears evidence of violence and abuse targeting Indigenous students and teachers

Sarah Collard

The federal inquiry into racism, hatred and violence directed at Indigenous peoples is continuing in Melbourne, with unions and national education and training organisations giving evidence.

The committee heard evidence about the lack of cultural safety in Australian schools and universities for First Nations educators and students. Research indicated that at least 20% of Indigenous teachers who left the profession did so because of racism and discrimination.

Witnesses giving evidence raised concerns about a chilling impact on reporting racist incidents at universities, citing fears about speaking out, harmful or inappropriate curricula in schools and the over representation of Indigenous students excluded from educational settings.

The committee heard evidence of targeted racist graffiti against an Indigenous teacher and emails from educators questioning the existence or impact of Stolen Generations policies, which forcibly removed tens of thousands of Aboriginal children from their families until the 1970s.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me! Achol Arok will be your guide into the weekend. Take care.

Three people charged, six in custody after alleged assault of Townsville boy

Three people have been charged and six others arrested after an alleged serious assault of a boy in Townsville last month.

Queensland police said the 17-year-old boy was found with serious injuries on 18 July in bushland after he was allegedly assaulted and tied to a tree. He was taken to the hospital in stable condition.

After investigations, officers charged three people, including a boy, 13, a woman, 35, and a girl, 14. They face charges including unlawfully detaining or confining, assault occasioning bodily harm and torture.

On Friday morning, six other people were taken into custody in relation to the investigation. They have not been charged.

Kat Wong

‘Overjoyed’: Police drop charges against protesters arrested at 2024 coal port blockade

More than 100 protesters who were arrested after blockading the world’s largest coal port in 2024 have had their charges dropped.

NSW police on Friday confirmed charges relating to Rising Tide’s 2024 demonstration at Newcastle port had been withdrawn.

Imala Cush, who had just finished high school when she was arrested at the protest, celebrated the result.

I’m overjoyed.

This has been a weight for the past two years and to finally have them dropped gives me hope for the climate movement and the strength of protests as a whole in this country.

The government cannot scare us away from fighting for a future.

Others who were arrested at the blockade said police should have withdrawn the charges earlier. Ecologist Susan Duncan said it would have “saved a lot of people time and heartaches”.

Almost 200 people were arrested as they paddled into the shipping channel in kayaks to prevent vessels from travelling through the Port of Newcastle.

Most of the arrested protesters were charged with operating a vessel to interfere with others’ use of waters and causing obstruction to a major facility, which could result in up to two years in prison.

A NSW police spokesperson said the decision to withdraw the charges followed a “review of the outstanding matters, taking into account the outcomes of cases already determined by the court and the available evidence in the remaining prosecutions”.

Matters from the 2025 Rising Tide event remain before the courts.

Petra Stock

Melbourne Royal Show monitoring bird flu situation before September event

Organisers of the Melbourne Royal Show say they are monitoring the evolving H5 bird flu situation before the event, planned for 24 September to 4 October.

The show’s general manager, Hannah von Bibra, said organisers would take all necessary measures to ensure the safety and well being of animals, exhibitors and visitors.

We are monitoring the H5N1 avian influenza situation, and are working closely with Agriculture Victoria, the Melbourne Royal Poultry Committee and veterinary advisers to assess the potential risks as it unfolds in Victoria.

We recognise this is an evolving situation and will continue to work closely with Agriculture Victoria and industry experts to ensure any decisions prioritise animal welfare and the safety of all involved.

The comments followed an announcement that South Australia’s Royal Adelaide Show had cancelled all bird shows and exhibits as H5 bird flu numbers continued to rise.

Adeshola Ore

Australia’s $50,000 parent visa takes so long to process that applicants die waiting

Wait times for visas to bring parents to Australia are so long that more than 1,500 applicants died before receiving their visa over a 21-month period to 31 March, new Department of Home Affairs data shows.

Reports of an upcoming overhaul of the nation’s migration system, including tougher rules for family visas, has intensified worry among Australians whose parents are waiting for their visas to be processed.

For applicants of non-contributory parent visas, which provide permanent residency for a fee of just under $9,000, the wait times are now an estimated 33 years.

Contributory parent visas have waiting times of about 15 years but cost almost $50,000 each.

Read more here:

Complainant J cross-examined about stays at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm

Amanda Meade

Back in the Alan Jones trial, complainant J has told the court he stayed at the broadcaster’s farm at Fitzroy Falls on two occasions.

Under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, J told the court he remembered a well-known tennis player being a fellow guest but not another athlete.

Bashir asked during cross-examination: “Were you ever at a barbecue with [them]?”

J replied: “No.”

J told the court he did remember the tennis player being a guest, although he didn’t know who they were at the time.

Bashir is challenging J’s memory of his visits to the southern highlands property, suggesting in court he had mixed up the occasions and the dates.

J agreed his family was invited to visit the property and that he accompanied them. Bashir is challenging him about how many nights he stayed at the property and which vehicle he was driving.

The court is now in recess for lunch. The trial continues.

Amanda Meade

Back to the Alan Jones trial

The cross-examination of complainant J in Alan Jones’s indecent assault trial in Sydney’s Downing Centre local court is continuing.

Jones’s barrister, Gabrielle Bahsir SC, is putting to J that the defendant did not sit on a couch in the lounge room of his Fitzroy Falls property wearing a bathrobe, and Jones didn’t enter J’s guest bedroom, as the complainant alleged in court earlier this week.

Bashir said during cross-examination: “He wasn’t in your bedroom, was he?”

“Yes, he was,” J replied.

J struggled to recall parts of the evidence he gave earlier this week about the alleged indecent assaults at Fitzroy Falls, which he says took place on the couch, in the bedroom and at a pigsty.

Bashir said in court: “Are you prepared to accept you had no basis to give that evidence that Mr Jones spoke to you in a ‘passionate voice’ and pulled you in for a cuddle?”

J replied: “No, I just don’t remember it right now.”

Bashir put it to J that none of his accounts, including the alleged kissing and “penis wiggle”, ever happened. The complainant insisted in court that it all happened as he’d described.

J agreed with Bashir that he did not protect himself by barricading himself in his room or pushing Jones off him.

J told the court during cross-examination: “I didn’t [push him off] … I was very scared. In that room I was as scared as I’ve ever been. It’s like you don’t have control of your body. I was very scared.”

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching involving six men.

Major delays and cancellations across Sydney airport due to air traffic control staff issues

Achol Arok

Travellers on domestic and international flights at Sydney airport have faced major delays and cancellations after Airservices Australia reported “operational restrictions to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands”.

Delays of up to 120 minutes were recorded across 75 Qantas and Jetstar flights, as well as four cancellations. Virgin Australia saw delays across 50 flights, while Rex was forced to off-load passengers after delays of up to an hour on the tarmac.

Airlines were advised the disruption was caused by staffing shortages at Airservices Australia.

The Airlines for Australia and New Zealand chief executive, Stephen Beckett, said the disruptions are unacceptable and “enough is enough”.

We need Airservices Australia to step up and support their traffic controllers to make sure there are enough of them, and their rosters are robust enough to make sure that this type of delay and disruption stops occurring.

The national network cannot grind to a halt because two or three people call in sick.

Airservices said the air traffic flow management measures had since been removed and “no further significant delays are anticipated”.

Attorney general writes to privacy commissioner about smartglasses concerns

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has written to the privacy commissioner over potential concerns surrounding smartglasses.

Rowland said the products, which are growing in popularity, had significant implications, especially for women and children who could be disproportionately affected by “inappropriate recording, harassment, surveillance or other harmful conduct”.

Rowland said in a statement:

Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear.

Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.

The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: climate protest charges dropped; Hanson’s media attack; and not looking back in anger
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon. Police have dropped charges against more than 100 climate protesters two years after they blockaded the port of Newcastle – the largest coal port in the world.

Dr Elizabeth Manning, a neuroscientist from Newcastle who faced two charges, including one carrying a $22,000 fine or two years in prison if prosecuted, said the action against the protesters had been “undemocratic”.

Climate Defenders Australia, a legal group representing the bulk of the protesters, said despite charges being dropped, “Australia leads the world for arresting climate protesters. That statistic alone is alarming – but it captures nothing of the long, anxious road that follows for those who then have to navigate the criminal justice system”.

Top news

  • Pauline Hanson echoes Trump as she lashes out about ‘fake news’ reporting on lavish London hotel

  • Complainant wants to ‘humiliate’ Alan Jones by revealing intimate details of alleged assaults, defence tells court

  • Man dies after suspected dog attack at rural property in Sydney suburb

  • Houthi strikes kill dozens in Yemen, officials say, as Saudi Arabia warns of further attacks

  • ‘Orange elephant in the room’: Pauline Hanson’s political rise is inspiring racism, inquiry hears

In pictures

Two former Iranian footballers, Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, said they were proud to have been granted Australian citizenship after being called traitors at home for refusing to sing the national anthem before a game.

What they said …

“The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.” – Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke

Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.

Podcast

Can the government really get ahead of the curve on AI? – Australian Politics podcast

On Wednesday, the Labor government announced environmental and energy safeguards on new datacentres in Australia. Our political editor, Tom McIlroy, speaks with Dr Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy, about the government’s push for national standards on datacentres.

Before bed read

Is becoming overwhelmed by feelings of nostalgia a bad thing?

Advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith says there’s a difference between longing for the past and assuming it was better.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: EGIS. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”

world.title: Nigerian security forces free more than 300 hostages in ‘largest single-day recovery’
world.snippet: President hails operation to rescue captives held in dense forests of Kainji Lake national park in north-central region Nigerian security...
world.content:
Nigerian security forces have rescued more than 300 abducted people in what the president, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, hailed as the largest single-day hostage recovery in the country’s history.

The release was announced on Wednesday after a joint operation, conducted by the military, police and counter-terrorism units, freed victims held captive in the dense forests of the Kainji Lake national park in the north-central region.

Among those who regained freedom were 163 people abducted in February during a deadly raid on the village of Woro in Kwara state, and 145 others seized primarily from the neighbouring Niger state. Both states are flanked to the west by Benin, where militant attacks have been surging in recent times. Officials confirmed the survivors are receiving medical evaluations at an army installation before being reunited with their families.

“The successful execution of this intelligence-led operation demonstrates the growing efficiency and collaboration among our security services,” Tinubu said in a statement on the presidency’s website. “I commend our gallant men and women in uniform for their bravery and unwavering commitment to safeguarding Nigerian lives.”

The government spokesperson Bayo Onanuga said the rescue operation was part of the president’s resolve to “restore lasting peace across every corner of the nation”.

In the last decade, kidnapping for ransom has become endemic in Africa’s most populous country, especially in the north where different armed groups including bandit gangs and jihadists roam large unoccupied forests and shrublands.

Between July 2024 and June 2025, at least 4,722 people were kidnapped across 997 reported incidents, leading to at least 762 deaths, according to a report by the Lagos-based geopolitical advisory SBM Intelligence. In that 12-month period, abductors demanded ₦48bn ($35m or £26m) in payments, with families and communities ultimately handing over at least ₦2.57bn in ransom to secure the release of their loved ones.

Ahead of January’s presidential election in which Tinubu is seeking a second four-year term, the government has been ramping up reforms and rescue operations as insecurity worsens.

The latest rescue was announced in the same week the army declared the governor of Islamic State West Africa Province, Abu Musa al-Mangawi Baa Shuwa, and his deputy, Amirul Jaish Muhammad Jidda, wanted. The duo run the Islamic State-affiliated Boko Haram offshoot operating primarily around the Lake Chad basin, which straddles Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Nigeria.

In July, security services freed at least 40 students and teachers who had been kidnapped in May from a school in Oyo in south-western Nigeria.

Last week, the presidency announced a salary increase worth 30% to 80% for thousands of soldiers, the largest hike in years for an army once seen as one of the continent’s most powerful but now derided as underfunded and unequipped to handle concurrent insurgencies across Nigerian territory.

world.title: ‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disaster
world.snippet: Washington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly influx into tiny Spanish territory The cosy relationship ...
world.content:
The cosy relationship between Washington and Rabat has long been flaunted by both sides, from Morocco’s announcement this year that it would be the first African state to join Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to the congratulatory message recently sent by Trump to mark King Mohammed VI’s 27 years in power.

The latest example landed this week. As Spain grappled with the aftermath of the sudden influx – and swift return – of more than 70,000 people into Ceuta, Morocco’s monarch confirmed he had named a $1bn highway flanking the disputed territory of Western Sahara after Trump.

The deepening ties have come under renewed scrutiny as questions continue to swirl over what exactly led to the deadly mass border crossing into the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.

“I think there’s enough evidence to hypothesise or claim that Morocco is behind this,” said Riccardo Fabiani, the north Africa project director for the International Crisis Group. “But there was no clear trigger for this, and this is what is puzzling for everyone.”

Observers have suggested Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s archrival, Algeria, could have set off Morocco. But another, perhaps more plausible explanation pointed towards the US, said Fabiani.

“It’s obviously impossible to demonstrate,” he said. “But in terms of plausibility, I don’t think it’s impossible to imagine that Morocco might have done something to earn brownie points with its allies, given that Morocco and this particular administration in Washington do have a very close, excellent relationship.”

While Morocco had probably not “masterminded” the surge into Ceuta, he said, its relationship with the Trump administration – along with the Moroccan king’s desire to keep its claim to Ceuta in the spotlight – may have affected how it responded to fast-spreading online rumours about the Spanish border being thrown open.

“For sure the Moroccan security forces were monitoring those conversations,” said Fabiani. “They saw that and there was probably some conversation where they decided to do nothing and see where this goes.”

What followed made headlines across the globe as tens of thousands of people swam or waded across one of the EU’s two land borders with Africa. As Spain scrambled to cope, far-right voices seized on the images.

In the US, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the state department blamed the influx on the Socialist-led government of Spain, while Trump warned that electing Democrats would make what happened in Spain “look small-time”. At no point did any of them mention Morocco or the potential role it might have played.

Trump and his administration have long been open about the deep antipathy they feel for Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, whose refusal to allow the US to use its airbases during the Iran war, rejection of the 5% defence spending target and vociferous criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza have arguably made Spain the administration’s least favourite EU country.

The American response seemed to be a triumph for Rabat, whose relationship with the US president traces back to his first term, when Morocco agreed to normalise ties with Israel in exchange for Trump’s recognition of its sovereignty claim over the disputed territory of Western Sahara.

Since then, Morocco’s all-powerful monarch had doubled down on outreach efforts, said Fabiani. “The Moroccans have really made extra efforts to cultivate every single major decision-maker within the administration, including the president himself, to make sure that this administration will support, until the end, the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.”

A hint that the relationship could help Morocco lay claim to more than Western Sahara came in a recent US congressional report that appeared to be sympathetic to Morocco’s refusal to recognise Ceuta as Spanish territory, describing it as “Spanish-administered” rather than a part of Spain, as it has been since 1580.

Days after the influx, interest in Ceuta remained heightened among those close to both Trump and the Israeli government, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, the director of the Madrid-based Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies. “They haven’t stopped talking about Ceuta for several days in a row, which is quite striking.”

What had been laid bare was Rabat’s willingness to use “hybrid tactics to achieve political objectives”, said Amirah-Fernández, drawing a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls to allow more than 8,000 people to cross into Ceuta in a show of anger over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara pro-independence leader to travel to Spain to be treated for Covid-19.

This time around, as nearly 10 times more people crossed into Ceuta, it set off a bout of finger-pointing across the EU rather than any kind of concerted effort to push back using the bloc’s status as Morocco’s largest trading partner and largest foreign investor. “The reaction of several governments in the EU was, in the end, what the White House was looking for – the erosion of solidarity between European partners,” said Amirah-Fernández.

Senior officials in Morocco have pushed back against accusations it was in any way complicit.

At the Rabat-based Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, there was little doubt that relations between Morocco and the US were in their “golden era”. Even so, the country’s approach to the Trump administration remained pragmatic, said Said Saddiki, a senior fellow at the institute.

“Moroccan policymakers are well aware of President Trump’s transactional style and have sought to preserve Morocco’s strategic autonomy,” Saddiki said in an email, citing efforts to maintain partnerships with the EU, China and the Gulf states, among others.

“The relationship with the Trump administration has strengthened Morocco’s international position, but so far it has not come at the expense of its relations with Spain or the European Union.”

For Fabiani, the events in Ceuta served to underscore the perils of Europe’s reliance on north African states to control migration flows. “This has made Europe entirely vulnerable and dependent on the goodwill of a country like Morocco,” he said. “Morocco is a partner, but at the same time it has its own interests. This vulnerability was on show.”

This weakness could become more of an issue as time passed, given Morocco’s perception that the issue of Ceuta remained unsettled, Fabiani warned. “And Morocco feels emboldened, and there is an administration in Washington that is willing to back it up,” he said. “I don’t think Europe is ready for what comes next because it could get much more complicated.”
